-   Read in the datasets

```{r}
# Read the data
# NOTE: belong, extraversion and neuroticism have had a small amount of random noise
# ("jitter") added to make them truly continuous (belong: 0-6; personality: 0-5)
df0 <- read.csv("https://daviddliebowitz.github.io/EDUC643_27W/data/belonging.csv")

# You can look at the variables and their types using this function
glimpse(df0)

## To see what each variable means, look at the codebook the study authors posted:
## https://daviddliebowitz.github.io/EDUC643_27W/data/belonging_codebook.xlsx

## Variables that start with t1__ were measured the summer before college;
## variables that start with t2__ were measured at the end of the first year.

## Some variables are categorical, but stored as numbers. You can see their values using

table(df0$t1__generation_br_combined_recoded)  # 0 = Unknown, 1 = First gen, 2 = Continuing gen
table(df0$college_name)
```

For this lab, we will focus on only continuous predictors. Let's subset to the relevant continuous predictors. There are individual survey items as well as composite scores, and we'll select the end-of-first-year (t2) composites for each of the Big Five personality traits.

```{r}
df0 <- df0 %>%
  select(Study_ID = token_var,
         belong = t2__dv_composite__belonging,
         extraversion = t2__dv_composite__personality_extrovert,
         neuroticism = t2__dv_composite__personality_neuroticism,
         agreeableness = t2__dv_composite__personality_agreeable,
         conscientiousness = t2__dv_composite__personality_conscientious,
         openness = t2__dv_composite__personality_open) %>%
  drop_na()
```

#### Task 3: Produce a correlation matrix and heatmap to assess for potential multicollinearity

-   Correlation matrix

```{r}
# Write the name of your dataset instead of the dots.

# datasummary_correlation(...,
#                         fmt = 3,
#                         notes = "Notes: cells report Pearson correlation coefficients.")
```

-   Easy correlation heatmap

```{r}
## Save correlations in a matrix using the cor() function
## Here I', removing the first column as that corresponds to the Study_id df0[,-1] 
cormat <- round(cor(df0[,-1]),3)
cormat
## We can use the corrplot package

#install.packages("corrplot")
corrplot::corrplot(cormat)
```

```{r}
## More complex using ggplot
cormat_df <- cormat %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column(var = "Variable1") %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -Variable1,
               names_to = "Variable2",
               values_to = "correlation")

ggplot(cormat_df, aes(Variable2, Variable1, fill = correlation)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#4a969e", high = "#d15e81", mid = "white",
                       midpoint = 0, limit = c(-1,1), space = "Lab",
                       name="Pearson\nCorrelation") +
  labs(x = "", y = "") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
```
